query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In an initially single‐phase high‐entropy alloy, high local stresses during deformation at intermediate temperatures drive the rapid nanosegregation of several principal elements (e.g. Ni, Cr, and Mn) to the grain boundaries. This clustering reduces local grain‐boundary cohesion and promotes brittle intergranular fracture even though the alloy remains nominally single‐phase. Engineering the grain boundaries to contain pre‐existing secondary phases or morphologically serrated features can sequester these segregating elements, mitigating the decohesion and thereby preserving toughness.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogeneous, single‐phase high‐entropy alloy (e.g., equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi or similar composition) with a refined microstructure.
generation.intervention: Compare two processing routes: one that retains conventional straight grain boundaries, and a second that uses a grain-boundary engineering treatment (e.g., a controlled heat treatment to promote in situ precipitation of embrittling-element–rich secondary phases or inducing serrated grain boundary morphology).
generation.conditions: Deformation tests performed at intermediate temperatures (e.g., 500–700°C) and loading rates that promote significant dislocation activity and diffusion without triggering conventional intermetallic formation.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundaries where nanosegregation/nanoclustering of principal elements occurs; alternatively, modified grain boundaries with pre‐existing secondary phases or a serrated morphology.
generation.mechanism: Under intermediate-temperature deformation, the interaction between moving dislocations and the severe lattice distortion characteristic of HEAs accelerates the diffusion and local accumulation of principal elements at grain boundaries. This targeted enrichment reduces the cohesive strength of the boundaries, leading to brittle intergranular crack initiation. By pre-establishing secondary phases at the boundaries (or modifying their morphology to be serrated), these embrittling species can be sequestered away from critical cohesive sites, thus preserving ductility and toughness.
generation.predicted_outcome: The untreated (straight GB) alloy will show a marked reduction in toughness and increased intergranular cracking correlating with the appearance of nanosegregation of principal elements at GBs. In contrast, the engineered alloy with preexisting GB modifications will display higher ductility and toughness under identical test conditions, with reduced evidence of detrimental segregation at the boundaries.
generation.baseline: The as-processed, single-phase HEA with uniformly distributed principal elements and straight grain boundaries.
generation.boundary: Predictions apply under service conditions where rapid dislocation movement and moderate diffusion occur (intermediate temperatures) and might not hold at very low temperatures (where cryogenic twinning dominates) or at very high temperatures (where conventional grain growth or intermetallic formation could become significant).
generation.uncertainty: While evidence from PMC6897545 indicates that nanosegregation of principal elements can lead to grain boundary decohesion, and PMC11407990 suggests that deformation-induced segregation is sensitive to strain rate and temperature in refractory HEAs, it remains uncertain how quantitatively these effects balance in different HEA compositions. The exact temperature window and kinetics of segregation in single-phase HEAs are not yet fully delineated.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of the same single-phase HEA. Process Set A with a standard heat treatment that yields straight grain boundaries. Process Set B with a modified heat treatment designed to induce either preformed Cr-rich precipitates at the grain boundaries or a serrated grain boundary morphology. Subject both sets to tensile and creep tests at intermediate temperatures (e.g., 600–700°C). Use atom probe tomography and high-resolution TEM to examine the chemical composition and morphology of grain boundaries in both sets before and after deformation.
measurements: Tensile ductility and toughness (fracture toughness, elongation to failure)
Creep rupture life and strain distribution
Grain-boundary chemistry via APT (extent of principal element nanosegregation)
Grain boundary morphology characterization via TEM/SEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the untreated set (straight GB) does not show significant grain-boundary segregation of principal elements or if its toughness degradation at intermediate temperatures is similar to that of the engineered set (modified GB), then the proposed mechanism—that decohesion by deformation-induced nanosegregation of principal elements is responsible for brittle behavior in single-phase HEAs—would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are novel high-temperature structural materials based on the design concept of high-entropy alloys (HEA) [, , ]. The multi-principal element characteristic of RHEAs leads to unique microstructures and remarkable properties, such as extremely high melting points, excellent high-temperature strengths, outstanding thermal stabilities, and exceptional creep, corrosion, and oxidation resistances [, , , ]. Owing to these advantages, RHEAs not only exhibit a significant application potential in aerospace and nuclear energy industries as high-temperature load-bearing or thermal protection structures, but also are regarded as an important development direction of high-temperature structural materials. Considering the crucial influence of microstructures on the properties, microstructure control is a meaningful approach to optimize and improve the macroscopic properties of alloys [,]. The element grain boundary segregation structure proposed in recent years provides extraordinary advantages to enhance the properties of alloys [,]. cited_evidence.text: Although the ductility of the dual-phase HEA is lower than the single-phase HEA at the testing temperature below 500°C, the ductility of the dual-phase HEA is greater than the single-phase HEA at 600° and 700°C. No intergranular embrittlement is observed. Figure 5 (B and C) shows the lateral surface in the vicinity of the fracture after tensile tests at 500° and 700°C, respectively. Figure 5 (D and E) exhibits typical ductile dimples on fracture surfaces after tensile tests at 500° and 700°C, respectively. In contrast to single-phase samples (Fig. 3D), the dual-phase sample has very few cracks near the lateral fracture surface. This suggests that the GB segregation engineering strategy via preexisting Cr-rich precipitates is effective to evade ductility loss at intermediate temperatures in HEAs. This is because the embrittling elements—such as Cr, Mn, or Ni—can be absorbed by preexisting embrittling element–enriched precipitates at GBs, which only leads to the growth of precipitates rather than GB embrittlement. However, when testing temperature was increased to 650°C, a significant hot ductility drop was observed for HT-1 sample. According to Figure 7(b), the facet cleavage surface and the limited amount of plastic deformation indicate that the failure mechanism was brittle intergranular fracture. The brittleness of HT-1 sample was even more pronounced under creep at 650°C as the creep fracture strain was only 0.03%. Cleavage edges on crept fracture surface (Figure 9(b)) and crack propagation along straight grain boundary (Figure 10(b)) indicate the vulnerability of straight grain boundary in HT-1 samples at elevated temperature. According to the local strain concentration at triple junctions of grain boundaries (Figure 11(a)), it is probable that HT-1 samples encountered an embrittlement at 650°C. The initiation of creep damage of HT-1 sample was a result of vacancy coalescence on grain boundaries perpendicular to the loading direction and severe strain concentration at grain boundaries.
